title: The Morning-Light Fix
twist: Most people try to fix a late bedtime at night. Sofia's fix came from the other end of the day: bright light in the morning pulled her body clock earlier.
briefing: Sofia, 16, can't fall asleep before 1 a.m. on school nights, even when she goes to bed at 10. Then her coach moves practice to 6:30 a.m., outdoors at sunrise, for two weeks. By the second week she is yawning at 10:30 p.m. and asleep within minutes.
question: How did an early morning practice fix her nights?

clues.title: Awake till 1 a.m.
clues.text: Even in the fall, when 4 p.m. swim practice wore her out, she lay awake until about 1 a.m. Going to bed earlier just meant more time staring at the ceiling.
clues.shows: a body clock running late, even when she was physically tired

clues.title: Dark mornings
clues.text: In winter she leaves for school in the dark and spends the day indoors. Her bedroom blinds stay shut until noon on weekends.
clues.shows: almost no bright light in her mornings

clues.title: Sunrise practice
clues.text: For two weeks, practice starts at 6:30 a.m. on an open field as the sun comes up. She is out in bright light for about an hour every morning.
clues.shows: a big dose of bright morning light every day

visual.unit: minutes of morning daylight, before → practice weeks

clues.title: Sleepy by 10:30
clues.text: By the second week she feels sleepy around 10:30 p.m. and falls asleep fast. It happened gradually over several days, not on the first night.
clues.shows: her sleepy time moving earlier, day by day

hypotheses.text: Bright light in the morning resets her brain's body clock earlier each day, so her sleep signal arrives earlier at night; dark mornings had let the clock drift late.
Practice tires her out, so she is exhausted by evening.
hypotheses.flaw: Hard afternoon swim practice tired her out last fall and she still lay awake until 1 a.m. — tiredness alone didn't move her bedtime.

hypotheses.text: She just got used to the early alarm.
hypotheses.flaw: Getting used to an alarm doesn't make you sleepy earlier at night — that's the body clock moving, and it only moved once her mornings got bright.

hypotheses.text: She is worried about practice, so she goes to bed early to be ready.
hypotheses.flaw: Going to bed early never worked before — she just lay awake. What changed is that she actually feels sleepy earlier.

prediction.prompt: After two weeks of the routine, how far earlier does Sofia's body clock shift as her daily dose of bright morning light goes from none to a full hour?

second.question: And the time she spends lying awake at night?

transfer.context: After a summer of sleeping until noon, Ben dreads the first week of school. His sister suggests he eats breakfast on the sunny porch every morning for the week before school starts.
options: Breakfast food makes you sleepy at night.
Fresh air will tire him out.
Bright morning light will pull his body clock earlier, so he gets sleepy at a normal bedtime.
It's a nice habit, but it can't change when he feels sleepy.
transfer.retryHint: What changed in Sofia's mornings before her bedtime moved?
transfer.explanation: The porch gives Ben what sunrise practice gave Sofia: bright light first thing every morning. That light nudges his body clock earlier day by day, so after a week his sleep signal arrives near a school-night bedtime.

takeaway: Your body clock is set by light. Bright light in the morning pulls it earlier, so sleepiness arrives earlier at night — the best fix for a late bedtime starts at sunrise.
